objectives: Define mate selection and tell attraction, preference and decision apart.
Describe how proximity, similarity and conversation shape who people actually meet.
Explain where age preferences come from, and name the mechanisms that can produce an age gap.
Tell a stated preference from a revealed one, and read the direction and the size of an age gap.
Separate deal-breakers from preferences, and name the trade-offs in your own choice.
Use plain sentences to talk about types, about age, and about what matters to you.

sections.body:
**Mate selection** is the process of choosing a partner. The word covers everything from the first moment of interest to the last decision to build a life with somebody. It is a process and not a single event: it can take weeks or years, it can be decided in an afternoon, and it can also end without a decision at all. Where the subject is studied, it is studied as a process with parts, because the parts can be checked separately and they do not always point the same way.

Three words have to be kept apart, because English uses them almost interchangeably. **Attraction** is the pull towards somebody: it is felt, it arrives fast, and it says nothing about the future. A **preference** is what a person says they want before any particular person appears: it is stated, it can be examined, and it can be wrong. A **decision** is the act of choosing one person out of the people who are actually available. A person can be attracted to somebody outside every preference they hold, and can prefer somebody they never choose.

This is why the distance between what a person looks for and what a person chooses matters more than either list on its own. A person looks for a set of qualities: a shared language, a shared way of working, a certain kind of humour, a family they can sit with. A person then chooses one individual, in one week, out of the people they actually meet. The list is a description of a wish. The choice is a decision made under conditions, and the conditions — the people you see, the time you have, the money you have — are not yours to choose alone.

This article gives you three things: the mechanism of the choice, the vocabulary other people use when they describe it, and a short procedure you can run on your own preferences. It does not tell you what kind of partner to look for, and it does not claim that one answer is better than another.
examples: Attraction is what you feel; preference is what you say; the decision is what you do.
The list is a wish, and the choice is made under conditions.
Mate selection is a process with parts, and the parts do not always agree.

sections.body:
In an interview, people give a clean list of reasons: looks, conversation, shared values, a sense of humour, work that feels useful, a family they get on with. The list is usually short, usually sensible, and usually sorted by importance. The behaviour is less tidy. When the two are compared, the behaviour is the better guide, because behaviour is what happened and a list is only what a person was willing to say.

Four forces do most of the work. **Proximity** comes first: who is physically near you, in the same building, on the same shift, in the same class, at the same hour of the day. People do not choose from the whole population; they choose from the people they see. The second force is similarity — people tend to end up with people who resemble them in some way, in background, in work, in values, in the way they spend an evening. The third is conversation: whether two people can talk easily for an hour is a practical test that many people apply without naming it. The fourth is time: how long you have known each other, and how often you meet.

The people you can actually choose from form your **choice set**. It is a small set, and it is made of your life: your work, your street, your friends' friends, your family, your habits. A preference you never act on costs nothing. A preference you cannot act on, because the person is not in your choice set, is not a preference at work — it is a wish about somebody who does not exist in your week. This is the part people rarely check, because the choice set feels like the whole world while you are inside it.

**Courtship** is the period in which two people find out what the other one is like. It has its own timetable: first meetings, then hours together, then the first small problem that has to be handled. Some people end a courtship early, because the first meetings answered the question. Others take much longer, because the question they are answering needs more evidence. The length of a courtship is not a measure of interest. It is a measure of how much the two people need to know before they can decide.
examples: Proximity decides who is available; similarity decides who stays in the frame.
Your choice set is the people you actually meet, not everybody you can picture.
The list in the interview is what a person was willing to say; the behaviour is what happened.
The courtship took longer because the question needed more evidence.

sections.body:
An **age preference** is the range of ages a person thinks of as suitable when choosing a partner. Almost everybody has one, whether or not they have ever said it out loud. It is usually written as an **age range**: a lower bound and an upper bound, sometimes narrow, sometimes wide, sometimes expressed as a gap instead of two numbers. It is a starting point for the search, not a rule the choice has to follow.

Three things feed that range. The first is the peer group and the family: the couples a person grew up among, the pairs their friends are making, and the combinations the family approves or disapproves of. The second is the culture around them — what is normal in a community, what a family expects, what two people of the same age are assumed to be doing. The third is the shape of the population. As people get older, the number of single people at each age changes, so the range of ages actually available to them changes too, and it usually narrows. A range that feels like a preference on one side of life can be a constraint on the other.

An **age gap** is the difference in age between two partners, and it has two parts: the size of the difference and its direction. A gap is a number of years between two dates of birth. When couples are studied as a group, a common pattern is that partners resemble each other on age and on other measured things: age, schooling, place of living, kind of work. That pattern has a name, **assortative mating**. It is a description of a pattern in a group, not a verdict on any couple inside the group.

What the gap measures is small and exact: the distance between two ages. What it does not measure is large: the quality of a relationship, the happiness of the people in it, who decides what, who earns what, or what either person wanted. How much of the gap is a preference people carry, and how much is a property of the situation they are in, is still debated. The answers on offer are different: one says the gap shows a preference for a particular stage of life; another says it shows who was in the choice set at the time; another says it shows the norms of the group, reinforced over years. The evidence is not settled enough to choose between them, and this article does not try.
examples: The age range is two numbers, and the age gap is the distance between them.
Assortative mating is a pattern in a group, not a verdict on a couple.
The gap tells you the distance between two dates of birth, and almost nothing else.
How much of this is preference and how much is circumstance is still an open question.

sections.body:
Four words carry most of the practical meaning. The first is the **deal-breaker**: a quality whose absence ends the possibility, as opposed to a quality that only lowers the score. Most people have very few of them, and they are worth finding out, because a deal-breaker saves the time a preference wastes. A second set of words sits in the middle: a quality you would like, that you can live without, and that you notice is missing.

**Compatibility** is the word for how well two people fit together in ordinary life. It is not the same as chemistry, which is felt at once, and it is not the same as agreement about values. It is closer to pace: who calls when, how money is discussed, whether a quiet evening is restful or empty. Compatibility shows up in small repeated situations, which is why it is often visible before the big subjects are.

**Readiness** is the state of being ready to be in a relationship: the free time, the money, the emotional state, the sense of what the relationship would cost. Readiness is a state and not a character. A person can be ready this year and not ready next year, and the same person can be ready for one relationship and not for another. It is also the word that separates a wish from a plan.

The last word is a **trade-off**: what you give up in order to get something else that you want more. Trade-offs are ordinary in this subject, because no partner carries every quality at once. Waiting longer for a better fit costs years. Choosing a person nearby costs some of the range. Saying what matters to you early costs a little ease. Naming a trade-off is not a verdict on the choice; it is how two people find out whether they are making the same one.
examples: A deal-breaker ends it; a preference only lowers the score.
Compatibility shows up in the small repeated situations.
Readiness is a state this year, not a label on the person.
Name the trade-off, and check that both of you are making it.

sections.body:
Two words in this subject are easy to mix up in an argument, and one number is easy to over-read. This section sets them side by side. The first comparison is between what a person says they want and what a person actually chooses. The second is the two parts of an age gap: its size and its direction. The third is what a gap can tell you and what it cannot.

The first pair is the easiest to get wrong. A stated preference is an answer given before any particular person stands in front of you. A revealed preference is the pattern in what a person has actually chosen. Revealed behaviour is usually the better evidence, because it cost something: the person could have chosen otherwise. But it is still a description of choices made under conditions, and it is not a reading of anybody's mind.

The second pair is the age gap itself. The size is the number of years between two people. The direction says who is older. Both are easy to state and easy to check, which is exactly why they are so often used as a shortcut for something they do not contain.

The third comparison is the one to keep in a conversation about a couple. An age gap is a fact about two dates of birth. It is not a fact about the quality of the relationship, about the power inside it, or about what either person wants. A table of differences is a tool for a conversation, not a verdict on the people in it.
examples: Stated preference is what you say; revealed preference is what you chose.
The size of the gap is a number; the direction is a name for the older partner.
The gap is a fact about two dates of birth, and the rest is conversation, not measurement.

sections.body:
This procedure takes one evening and no tool. It does not produce an answer about another person; it produces a description of your own choice, and the description is the part you can check.

The first three steps put two lists next to each other. The next two separate the items that end a possibility from the items that only rank it. The last two name what you are giving up, and what you would say out loud. Write the answers down: an answer written in a sentence behaves differently from an answer held in the head.

The procedure is deliberately dull. It asks no question about anybody else's intentions, and it produces no score to compare with other people. If a step gives you a surprise, that is the point of the step.
examples: First the list I say, then the list I live.
A deal-breaker ends it; a preference only ranks it.
Write the trade-off down, and the surprise with it.
sections.heading: How to read your own preferences
steps: Write down what you say you want, as a plain list of qualities. Do not soften it and do not leave anything out.
Write down the last few people you actually spent time with who were possible partners, and note what they had in common.
Compare the two lists, and mark every item that is on the first list and missing from the second.
Sort each item into a deal-breaker or a preference, and ask of every deal-breaker: would this end it, or would it only lower the score? Move it if it belongs in the other column.
Name the trade-off: what do you give up to get the quality you rank first, and how long are you willing to pay for it?
Write your age range as two numbers, then write the age range of the people you actually meet. Write down the distance between the two without judging either of them.
Say it in one sentence to somebody who asks: what you want, what you will not accept, and what you are trading for it.

sections.body:
Three things are left out on purpose.

First, this article does not tell you what age to choose, or what age your partner should be. An age gap is a measurement of two dates of birth, and a measurement of that kind carries no verdict on a relationship, on a person, or on a life.

Second, the direction of an age gap has more than one explanation, and the explanations have not settled between them: the shape of the age range as people get older, the peer group and the family that supplied the model, the people you actually met, and the norms of the culture you live in. Any one of them can produce a similar pattern, and several of them act at the same time.

Third, none of this is a rule about whom you may love or whom you may live with. It is a description of a process and a vocabulary for it. Where the choice is yours to make, the information here is the kind that makes the choice clearer, and the choice stays yours.
examples: An age gap is a measurement, not a verdict.
Several mechanisms can produce the same direction, and the debate between them is open.
This article describes the process; it does not choose for you.
sections.heading: What this article does not tell you

sections.body:
The first three answer a friend who asks about types. The next three answer a comment about age. The last six are for a first meeting, or for a conversation with somebody you already like.

The voice is flat on purpose. A sentence about preferences that sounds like a verdict starts an argument about the verdict, and you want the argument to stay on the things that matter: the qualities, the boundaries, the trade-offs.
examples: I have an idea of what I want, but I would not call it a type.
What I look for is somebody I can talk to easily; the rest comes after that.
I do not keep a fixed list. Some things matter more than others, and I know which ones.
We are six years apart, and the age is not the part I worry about.
I know the age range people expect. My choice was not made on that range.
An age gap describes two dates of birth. It does not describe the relationship.
What I need most is somebody I can talk to for an ordinary evening.
For me the deal-breaker is unkindness; everything else is a preference.
I am looking for company I can keep, not a first impression I can repeat.
The trade-off is time: more choice now, or a settled life sooner.
My age range is wider than people expect, and I am comfortable with that.
I would rather meet the person first and decide later than set a rule and follow it blindly.
sections.heading: Sentences you can use

item.summary: Mate selection is the process of choosing a partner, and it has its own vocabulary. After reading this you can separate attraction, preference and decision, describe how people actually choose, read the direction and the size of an age gap, and run a short check on the preferences you say you hold.
item.title: Mate Selection and Age Preferences
